metadata.title: How are PISA results related to adult life outcomes?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief summarizes results from OECD’s longitudinal analysis of PISA performance and later adult outcomes, rather than presenting a new student-level ML model. The analytic approach relies on PISA 2018 reading performance at age 15 and follow-up outcomes around age 25 in a small set of countries (Australia, Canada, Denmark, Switzerland), using OECD’s previously published longitudinal evidence. The document does not report the specific complex-sampling weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be verified from the text provided. For replication with PISA microdata, analysts should apply the standard PISA complex survey design weights and replicate methods as provided in the OECD/IEA databases, and ensure that any longitudinal linkage uses the same weighting and missingness rules as in the underlying OECD report.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The brief reports descriptive longitudinal associations (e.g., university completion and skilled employment by PISA reading performance quartiles) rather than an achievement model that explicitly uses PISA plausible values (PVs) in a documented estimation procedure. Because the text does not describe an explicit PV-based scoring/estimation workflow for the reported comparisons, PV handling is treated as not applicable for this extraction. Missing-data handling is also not described in the provided text, so the specific strategy (e.g., complete cases vs. imputation) cannot be assessed from this brief alone.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief focuses on longitudinal follow-up in four countries that tracked students from the PISA 2000 or PISA 2003 cohorts into early adulthood (around age 25). It reports outcomes by quartiles of PISA reading performance at age 15 (top quarter vs bottom quarter) computed for the final longitudinal sample in each country. No additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., attrition handling, linkage completeness thresholds, or missing-outcome restrictions) are specified in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesizes longitudinal evidence linking PISA reading performance at age 15 to adult life outcomes around age 25. It highlights that students in the top quarter of PISA reading performance are substantially more likely to complete university and to be in skilled employment, and less likely to be NEET, compared with students in the bottom quarter, with large cross-country differences reported for Australia, Canada, Denmark, and Switzerland. The brief also reports that accounting for PISA reading performance reduces gaps in skilled employment between advantaged (tertiary-educated parents) and disadvantaged youth, suggesting that school performance is an important mediator of later labour-market inequality. Additionally, students’ expectations for high-skilled work and self-reported perseverance/effort in school are associated with later educational attainment, even after accounting for reading performance in at least one example. The document does not provide model-based ML metrics or a transparent PV/missing-data estimation procedure within the brief, so the results should be interpreted as descriptive longitudinal associations rather than as newly estimated predictive models.
